lessons.title: Building good working relationships
lessons.html:
Building good working relationships

Work in a seed plant, laboratory or research station is teamwork. The processing team depends on the receiving team, the laboratory depends on clean, labelled samples, and sales depend on everyone delivering on time. When relationships are good, work goes smoothly and problems are solved quickly. When they are poor, mistakes, delays and conflict follow.

What makes a working relationship effective

  • Respect: treat everyone with dignity, regardless of position, language, culture, gender, age or religion.
  • Trust: do what you say you will do. Be honest when you make a mistake.
  • Clear communication: say what you mean, listen carefully and check understanding.
  • Cooperation: help others when they are under pressure, for example during the planting season rush.
  • Fairness: share work and credit fairly.

Diversity in the workplace

South African workplaces bring together people of many languages and backgrounds. Diversity is a strength: different people bring different knowledge and ideas. The Employment Equity Act prohibits unfair discrimination at work. Avoid jokes, nicknames or comments that insult people's culture, race, gender or beliefs. If a colleague is not fluent in the language used, speak clearly, avoid slang and check understanding without talking down.

Communicating well

  1. Listen actively: give attention, do not interrupt, ask questions.
  2. Use the right channel: urgent safety issues face to face or by phone, routine information by e-mail or notice board.
  3. Confirm important instructions in writing.
  4. Give feedback that is specific and about the work, not the person: 'The labels on these bags are missing lot numbers' rather than 'You are careless'.

Your role as a team member or leader

At NQF level 4 you may lead a small team. Set a good example: arrive on time, follow safety rules, and support team members who are learning.

lessons.title: Handling conflict and problems
lessons.html:
Handling conflict and problems

Conflict happens in every workplace. It is not always bad: disagreement can lead to better ideas. Conflict becomes harmful when it is ignored, becomes personal or turns into bullying.

Common causes of conflict

  • Unclear roles or instructions
  • Unfair sharing of work or overtime
  • Poor communication or rumours
  • Pressure and long hours in peak season
  • Personal differences and misunderstandings

Steps to resolve conflict

  1. Act early. Do not wait for a small issue to grow.
  2. Talk privately with the person, at a calm time.
  3. Describe the problem using facts, not blame.
  4. Listen to the other person's view.
  5. Look for a solution that works for both.
  6. Agree on actions and follow up.
  7. If it cannot be solved, involve your supervisor or use the company grievance procedure.

Example

Two workers on the packing line argue because one often leaves early and the other must finish cleaning. The team leader meets both, hears each side, finds that the first worker has a transport problem, and arranges a fair cleaning roster. The problem is solved without disciplinary action.

What is never acceptable

  • Violence or threats
  • Sexual harassment
  • Bullying or victimisation
  • Unfair discrimination

These must be reported to management according to company policy. The Labour Relations Act and company disciplinary codes provide fair procedures for dealing with misconduct.

Supporting others

Notice when a colleague is struggling, for example with stress or a personal problem. Listen, and if needed suggest the employee assistance programme or a supervisor. Respect confidentiality.

Key points

  • Good working relationships are built on respect, trust, communication and cooperation.
  • Diversity is a strength; unfair discrimination is unlawful.
  • Give feedback about the work, not the person.
  • Deal with conflict early, privately and with facts.
  • Use the grievance procedure for unresolved issues and report harassment or violence.
